She stopped. She tried to focus past the lights and the cameras and the people waiting to speak. "I'm just...um...I'm just not sure how they'll get to school, or do their homework, or learn to read."

She heard Mei muttering something from behind her and then the words spilled out. "And I've lived in the U.S. for eleven years and Mrs. Ahn taught me how to read English and I think I owe everything to her." She managed to say that without crying.

And then, to her own surprise, she said, "I know you probably take this job very seriously, but this library is important to me -- and important to my kids. Thank you."

She let go of the microphone, stopped breathing, and sat back down. Mei patted her back.

The Westside branch stayed open.

The city council voted to close Westside Library anyway. *

The Westside branch had been open for thirty-nine years, the first library in the neighborhood after the riots.* When it closed, people lined up for the last day. They stood looking at shelves and remembering childhood visits and old teachers and help received. Mrs. Ahn sat behind the circulation desk and wept quietly.

A few months later Dana's daughter, Yumi, went to the new branch with her third-grade class. They took the bus downtown past the old Westside Library, now bricked up at the windows in case vandals tried again.

At the big new library downtown, Yumi was given a card, and they made a game of finding her favorite authors in the catalog and seeing if the books were on the shelf. Afterward, while their teacher was talking to the youth-services librarian, Yumi stood looking up at the third-floor windows. In her imagination she could see Mrs. Ahn setting out puzzles for the preschoolers, the boys in the afterschool chess club, a dozen kids listening spellbound to a story, a mother studying for her citizenship test. The shiny new building didn't change what she remembered, what she had loved at the Westside branch.

The next Saturday morning, when Yumi was still in bed and her brother was watching cartoons with his father, Dana Kim gathered her courage. She got out the two index cards and crossed off a few words. Then she walked over to the nearest library and asked if she could volunteer for a few hours one morning a week. She didn't care if it was shelving books or cleaning the bathroom. She just wanted to walk into a library and feel steady on her feet.

My sons go to Wilbur Waxman Middle School. Every Saturday I take them to story time at the Westside branch library. My name is Dana Kim and I beg you--please, please keep the library open. Every week, that library gives our children a place to--to feel like their brains matter. If it closes I don't know where they'll go, or where I'll go. So please."

Her chest ached. Mei had squeezed all the way to the end. Now her hands stopped trembling and she remembered her second card. "The librarian there, Mrs. Ahn, is like family to us."

That wasn't all she'd planned to say, but it was enough. The lights weren't as harsh now. She managed to look up as she stepped back from the podium, and for a second she thought she saw a nod from Joe Albright on the dais.

The room cracked open for her and let her walk out without shame.

On Thursday the council voted to close six branches, but not Westside.

At story time that Saturday Mrs. Ahn waved extra-special to Dana before she started the hour with "Goodnight Moon."

But tonight, walking home under the sodium lights with Mei's arm around her, she felt strangely lightheaded, as if the air coming into her lungs was just a bit sweeter. She'd done a hard thing, and she'd done it without struggling, without panicking.

Mrs. Ahn was standing alone, near a stack of boxes. She saw Dana and smiled. She was a short, slender woman in her late fifties, and her hair was completely white.

"What are you going to do?" Dana said. "With all these books."

"The children's books they're giving to the schools," Mrs. Ahn said. "The reference books and magazines are going to the public library next county over."

"And this other stuff," Dana said. "The fiction, the paperbacks?"

Mrs. Ahn shrugged. "They want me to throw it away." She made a motion to a stack of crates by the box: The Last Battle, The Enchanted Castle, The Buffalo Soldier's Groove.

"May I have them?"

"What are you going to do with your own copies?" Mrs. Ahn raised a speculative eyebrow.

"I'm not going to read them," Dana said. "I'm going to prop my windows open."

"You know what this means," Mrs. Ahn said to her. "The books are your responsibility once you take them. You can't ask me anymore about which is better, Dune or Foundation, or if Spenser gets Susan back. That's all on you now."

"Yes, ma'am," Dana said. She brought a cart and paper grocery bags and made a pile big enough to fill two of her drawers. She left Mrs. Ahn and the other library employees to pass on the books to anyone else who wanted them, and she took the cart out to her car and loaded her haul into the trunk. They made a fine block of bricks at the bottom.

When she got home, she started piling them up against the bottom half of the dining room windows. She had just enough for one. She didn't know why.
